title: Mean Girls
full_review:
An insecure 15-year-old, home-schooled for most of her life, gets a crash course in survival-of-the-social-fittest when she is thrust into a public high school in the catty teen comedy "Mean Girls" (Paramount).

Director Mark Waters reteams with his "Freaky Friday" leading lady, Lindsay Lohan, to craft a movie both breezy and biting, charting the treacherous psychological waters many high school-aged girls must navigate today. But, despite its frothy facade, the movie is laced with hard-edged sexual references (including a scene involving a sad-sack health education teacher distributing condoms to his class) which make it unsuitable for the 'tween and young teen audience it seems aimed at attracting.
Lohan plays Cady Heron, the "new girl" du jour whose at-home education in the African bush by her zoologist parents (Neil Flynn and Ana Gasteyer) has left her brainy but rather clueless when it comes to peer social skills. Of course, this wouldn't pose much of a problem had her parents decided to stay in the veldt. Instead, they move to Chicago and enroll Cady in a real school, where the wildlife is considerably more ferocious than anything the African continent has to offer.

On her first day of school, Cady, desperate for friends, hooks up with two social misfits, Janis (Lizzy Caplan), a goth gal rumored to be a lesbian (though the rumors are later proven false), and the flamboyant Damian (Daniel Franzese) -- no rumors needed -- who is "almost too gay to function."

Cady's fresh-scrubbed good looks also earn her the privilege of lunching with "the plastics," the school's preternaturally pretty ruling class, led by queen bee Regina (Rachel McAdams). Lacey Chabert and Amanda Seyfried round out the Barbie brigade, playing Regina's snooty sycophants. Though really not wanting to be co-opted into the catty clique, Cady is cajoled by Janis to infiltrate their ranks and report back with enough gossip to dethrone the teen tyrants. Her undercover mission proves only too successful, and in gaining popularity, Cady winds up hurting her friends in the process.

Adapted from the book "Queen Bees and Wannabes" by Rosalind Wiseman, the screenplay was written by "Saturday Night Live" performer and head writer Tina Fey, who plays Cady's math teacher. Fellow "SNL" cast members past and present fill in the supporting ranks, including Gasteyer as Cady's mother, Tim Meadows as the school's principal and Amy Poehler as Regina's bimbo mom.

Jonathan Bennett plays smart and sensitive Aaron, Regina's old flame. Cady commits the mortal sin of expressing interest in him, setting herself up for a lesson in Backstabbing 101.

Though not as dark as "Heathers" (1989), "Mean Girls" uses barbed wit to comment on the unwritten social rules and teen tribal customs that govern contemporary high school hierarchies. The film contains several amusing sequences where the African-raised Cady sees various interactions among her peers through a wildlife prism -- viewing, say, a crowded shopping mall fountain as a watering hole, with the teens gathered around it acting appropriately animalistic. A background sight gag concerning Regina's toddler sister proves the most perceptive observation made by the film, and makes a subtle but strong argument against using TV as a babysitter.

To its credit, while spending much of its time mocking the geeky, intellectually-inclined "mathletes," it is one of the few teen films that makes its heroine an academic all-star.

"Mean Girls" seems to go out of its way to promote a positive message about self-esteem and tolerance, including several syrupy sermons wrenched into the ending. Sadly, however, much of what is preached is just lip service, since the open-mindedness extended to certain groups -- the overweight, homosexuals etc. -- is denied to others, like Christian evangelicals and those who believe that abstinence is a valid option for teens.

Due to recurring crude language and humor, some drug references and implied underage drinking, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
